Great brief — it's unusually well-posed, and the erosion-distributes-over-intersection thickness check and the shared-vertical-axis decomposition are both genuinely elegant. My strongest single observation up front: **the same interval arithmetic you use for coverage also answers Q1 exactly, and likely deserves to be the backbone of Q3's ranking too.** Details below, question by question.

## Overall read on the brief

Two technical caveats before the questions:

- Your thickness check is a one-sided test. Erosion distributing over intersection is correct (and the infinite-extrusion identity \(E \ominus B(r) = (\Sigma \ominus D(r)) \times \mathbb{R}\) is exact), but "eroded solid non-empty" only certifies that *some* point has clearance \(r\) — a thin neck elsewhere passes silently. For "minimum wall everywhere," compare the solid against its opening: \(S \ne (S \ominus B(r)) \oplus B(r)\) flags any feature under \(r\). The residual no longer distributes as cleanly over intersection, so here it costs real 3D work; still cheap to run only on finalists.
- "A shadow can only lose ink, never gain it" holds while the object stays inside the visual hull of the target silhouettes; your rods/base plates already deliberately violate it within budget. Worth stating the invariant explicitly as "shadow ⊆ target ∪ allowed-extra," because Q1 hinges on exactly this hull boundary.

The font-dominance benchmark finding (Bungee 16/16 vs Arial 7/16) is excellent design-shopping data, and it becomes even more powerful in combination with the Q2 suggestion below, because font choice stops being discrete.

## Q1 — Hidden connectors

The headline result, stated precisely: a silhouette-legal connector between two pieces exists **if and only if both pieces lie in the same connected component of the full visual hull** \(V = E_F \cap E_S\), where \(E_F, E_S\) are the extrusions of the *whole-word* target silhouettes (not the per-cell silhouettes). \(V\) is the maximal volume whose projections stay inside both silhouettes; any path whose two projections stay inside letter ink is, by definition of the extrusions, confined to \(V\). So hidden-connectability is a connectivity query on \(V\), nothing more. Ranked approaches:

1. **Exact z-sweep connectivity (best).** Your key fact generalizes directly. A slice of \(V\) at height \(z\) factors as \(X_z \times Y_z\), where \(X_z = \{x : (x,z) \in \Sigma_F\}\) and similarly for \(Y_z\) — a slice is a product of two families of 1-D intervals, i.e., a union of axis-aligned rectangles. Connectivity over \(z\) reduces to tracking two interval families: components of adjacent slices merge iff they overlap in both \(x\) and \(y\). Sweep the silhouette-vertex heights, maintain union-find; exact, near-2D complexity, no voxels, no booleans. This is the same math that makes your coverage exact, one level up.
2. **Segment tests for short gaps.** A straight connector from \(p\) to \(q\) is legal iff its front projection is a segment contained in \(\Sigma_F\) and its side projection in \(\Sigma_S\) — two 2D segment-in-polygon checks (no boundary crossings). Sample candidate contact points on piece boundaries and test; this upgrades your MST rods into "hidden-qualified" rods, and any rod that passes contributes zero extra shadow instead of ≤3%.
3. **Rasterized fallback.** Voxelize \(V\) inside its bounding box (or sample SDFs), flood-fill components, pathfind within a component between contact sets, thicken the skeleton. Cruder but robust to anything. Only needed if the sweep's casework gets painful.

**Should connectivity steer the search? Yes**, and it's cheap if scoped: whether adjacent chain cells \(i, i{+}1\) are hidden-connectable through their shared neighborhood is a local property (restrict \(V\) to the slabs spanned by those two chunks) and can be computed as a per-edge feature inside your existing DP. Add "hidden links" to the Pareto front; reserve post-hoc rods for residual breaks. For fragments like the i-dot, the same test tells you when keeping the dot is *feasible* rather than merely preferring it — the "loose fragments" penalty becomes "fragment not hidden-connectable," which automatically rescues the title-case i paired with B **when** the hull genuinely routes through (the corridor must wander through *neighboring* letters' ink in the front view, since i itself has no ink between dot and stem — a good reason the routing must be global, not local to a cell). Pitfall: if you thicken connectors to meet wall thickness, pathfind in the *eroded* hull \(V \ominus B(r)\) so the thickened result is legal by construction.

## Q2 & Q3 — Deformation and ranking

For Q2, my top recommendation is a reframing: don't deform outlines with ARAP as the primary tool (ARAP being the Sorkine–Alexa local-rigidity framework Mitra & Pauly lean on ); instead, **search over the designer-sanctioned deformation space of a variable font**. Roboto Flex exposes parametric axes that are exactly your problem's coordinates: YTAS (ascender height), YTDE (descender depth), YTLC (lowercase zone), YTUC (uppercase), YTFI (figures), XTRA (counter width), YOPQ (vertical stroke). These axes encode years of decisions about how an i may stretch without ceasing to be an i — the legibility-preservation problem is pre-solved by the type designer. Full ranking: [dl.acm](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/34.273735)

1. Variable-font axes as the deformation basis; search/bake per-glyph or per-chunk axis values. roboto-delta even carries an avar2 fully-parametric build. [m3.material](https://m3.material.io/blog/roboto-flex)
2. OpenType stylistic/contextual alternates and case mixing (which you already do) as discrete "giant steps" in the same space.
3. Band-preserving z-stretch: treat ascender/x-zone/descender as separate bands, scale bands independently, keep stroke widths roughly constant. Crude approximation of YTAS/YTDE with any static font.
4. True ARAP skeleton deformation as last resort; known pitfall list: spikes at handles and energy-splitting artifacts. [github](https://github.com/googlefonts/roboto-delta)

For measuring legibility loss, one practical and one principled suggestion. Practical: render the candidate shadow and score it with an off-the-shelf letter classifier — an OCR model or a small letter CNN running via ONNX in your same JS environment gives a continuous "is this still an F" margin that doubles as a loss term. Principled: define distortion as distance in parametric-axis space (sum over letters of per-axis deviation from default, axis-normalized) — it's the most defensible "principled distortion measure for type" I know of, and with option 1 it costs nothing extra. For Q3's ranking policy, I'd propose: unfixable-fragment count → coverage → parametric-axis distance → extra shadow → compactness, then expose 2–3 scalarization sliders over the Pareto front interactively. Speculating: if you want to be obsessive, fit weights from pairwise human preference clicks with a Bradley–Terry model; I expect the interactive slider to win on effort-to-value.

## Q4 & Q5 — Layouts and oblique views

Q4: what reads as *designed* is alignment and repetition, so I'd add a post-layout "typographic discipline" pass ranked roughly: shared x-height enforced globally across both words (not just per row); optical spacing via whitespace equalization between stem pairs rather than equal advance widths (equalize the *areas* of the inter-letter counters — this is how type designers space, and it's a 2D distance-transform computation you already have ingredients for); stem-grid snapping, i.e., quantize stem centerlines across cells to a small set of shared column positions so the two words echo each other's rhythm; deliberate shared motifs (align all i-dots to one height, line up ascender tops) rather than per-chunk local decisions. The random stroke-pairing approach you cite from AmbigramGenerator reads as jumbled precisely because it lacks these global alignment lines. References worth absorption beyond that: John Langdon's *Wordplay* ambigrams and Scott Kim's *Inversions* for what "economy of means" looks like in letterform transformation.

Q5: mostly good news for your machinery. Any two *vertical* viewing directions still share the vertical axis — \(\vec n_1 \times \vec n_2\) is horizontal only if a wall tilts — so reparametrize the ground plane by \((u_1, u_2)\), each view's wall-parallel coordinate; the map from \((x,y)\) is linear and invertible for \(0 < \theta < 180°\), and a \(z\)-slice of the hull is *still* a product of two interval families (rectangles in \((u_1,u_2)\) space, parallelograms in \(xy\)). Coverage math and the Q1 connectivity sweep survive verbatim in the reparameterized frame. What changes: chain steps of \((\Delta, \Delta)\) project shorter in each view as \(\theta\) shrinks, so letters crowd toward overlap as \(\theta \to 0\) and everything degenerates at \(\theta = 0\); \(\theta \in [60°, 120°]\) should be near-equivalent by symmetry, with 45° just compressing cell spacing budgets. For three words at oblique azimuths, all vertical views still share \(z\), but slices become intersections of \(k\) strip families rather than a 2-fold product — the sweep survives, the slice combinatorics grow (hexagon-ish components), fine for two words plus a spine. The killer is a *top* word, as in the GEB corner itself : a horizontal viewing plane couples \(x\) and \(y\) jointly and breaks the product structure outright. Speculating on printability: sharper corners likely *help* piece count (slices are fatter along the bisector, more collision volume between pieces) but make the base plate geometry needier; I'd build the 45° end-to-end math check before trusting that. [arxiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.10335v1)

## Q6 — Search at scale

Ranked by effort-to-payoff, with three words in mind:

1. **CP-SAT (e.g., OR-Tools) with precomputed cell tables.** Your DP already factors cell quality from cell pairing; export per-(chunk_F, chunk_S, style-bucket) cost tables and declare chunk boundaries as integer variables with channeling constraints, coverage/street thresholds as feasibility cuts, lexicographic solve per Pareto point. Suddenly "three words" is three coupled alignments the solver handles relationally, and you get provable optimal-or-timeout behavior. Cache keys (letter-chunk pairs repeat heavily across names) do most of the work.
2. **Factor-graph composition of pairwise DPs.** Exact 3-way sequence alignment is NP-hard (classical sums-of-pairs MSA result, Wang & Jiang 1994), so don't build a cubic-time exact DP; instead run your existing pairwise alignments as factors on the three word-chains and reconcile with loopy min-sum belief propagation or dual decomposition. Elegant, reuses working code, no solver dependency —but debugging loopy BP convergence is its own tax, hence second.
3. **A\*/beam search over joint layouts** with admissible heuristics = sums of per-cell independent lower bounds (you can prove consistency from your 2D-arithmetic cell bounds; "a cell's coverage is exact alone and a lower bound in the chain"  is exactly what makes the heuristic admissible). Beam width gives anytime behavior.
4. Simulate-anneal only as a polisher over a solver-seeded start; learned heuristics last — you don't yet have the instance volume to train anything honestly, and the Q1 interval-sweep plus caches will embarrass an ML guesser at this scale.

Pitfalls across all: Pareto fronts blow up combinatorially — prune with ε-dominance per your existing 0.5% rounding discipline; and profile the manifold-3d booleans as the true bottleneck — precomputing cell geometry per repeated chunk pair should dwarf search-complexity concerns until names get very long. The space-carving lineage (Kutulakos & Seitz's "carve until photo-consistent" ) also suggests a cheap pre-pass: before any layout search, intersect eroded target hulls to certify feasibility per font, which turns your Bungee-vs-Arial benchmark into an automatic font screener. [arxiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.10335v1)

Happy to go deeper on any thread — the z-sweep union-find internals or a CP-SAT model sketch for the three-word case are the two I'd pick myself.
